How I Rebuilt My Body and Confidence After 40 — Lessons Beyond Fitness
At 38, I stepped on a bodybuilding stage for the first time.

It wasn’t about trophies — it was about taking back control of my body.
After two kids, a full-time career, and years of “diet starts Monday” cycles, I decided to see what was truly possible if I treated my body like it mattered.
What I learned:

Discipline is quieter than motivation.
 It’s showing up when no one’s watching.

Nutrition is not punishment.
 It’s an act of respect.

Progress isn’t linear.
 It’s built on hundreds of ordinary days done well.

Competing taught me something far beyond macros and reps.
 It taught me how to lead myself again — something many women lose track of after 35.

So no — you don’t need to get on stage.

But you do need to take your health seriously enough to feel powerful in your own skin again.
posts.hook: How I Rebuilt My Body and Confidence After 40 — Lessons Beyond Fitness

posts.text:
My father is 69. Three diagnoses, seven pills… and still tells me ‘I’m fine, don’t overthink.’”

 Retired. Two children doing well in their careers, life seemingly sorted from the outside.

High blood pressure.
Type-2 diabetes.
Thyroid numbers that fluctuate but are always described as “manageable.”
Cholesterol that no one brings up unless the report forces the conversation.

Seven pills a day.
Regular blood work.
And the same sentence every time I ask how he’s really doing — “I’m fine, don’t overthink so much.”

I tried everything a well-meaning, informed daughter would do.
Reminding him to walk.
Correcting food choices.
Forwarding articles.
Explaining why sugar spikes matter even when medicines are on board.

He listened.
Nodded.
And went back to the same chair, the same television, the same rhythm that slowly brought him here.

For a long time, I thought he was being stubborn.
Until I realised something uncomfortable.

His generation was never taught how to care for themselves — only how to carry responsibility quietly, ignore discomfort, and keep going no matter
what the body was asking for.

So I stopped trying to fix him.
And started changing the space around him.
Dinner moved slightly earlier, without calling it “healthy.”
One bowl of curd or dal became non-negotiable, without explaining protein.
Evening walks stopped being about steps and became about time together.
The phone went away at night, the TV stayed — sleep came easier.
 And I followed the same routines, so it never felt like instructions.
No strict diet.
No gym talk.
No fear-based warnings about the future.

Slowly, the sugar readings steadied.
BP became less erratic.
Digestion improved.
Sleep deepened.

But the biggest change wasn’t on paper.
It was in him.
Less irritability.
Less withdrawal.
More presence.

I learned this the hard way:
Indian parents don’t resist care.
They resist being treated like problems that need fixing.

If you’re a professional trying to take care of aging parents while balancing your own life, understand this — advice rarely works, but shared routines quietly do.

If this feels like your father too, comment “PARENTS” — I’ll DM a simple, sustainable starter guide that helps without arguments, guilt, or resistance.

Save this.
Send it to your sibling.
 Sometimes care has to look like respect before it looks like health.

“The arm around my shoulder lasted 5 seconds… and I wanted to freeze time.”

We were just taking a casual picture.
He came and put his arm around my shoulder for maybe 5 seconds.
That’s it.

I smiled for the camera, but inside something shifted.

Because if you’re a mother of a teenage son, you know these moments become rare, unexpected gifts.

There was a time when he would:

sit in my lap without invitation,
hold my hand everywhere,
tell me every random thing that happened in his day,
and hug me just because he walked past me.

Now he is taller than me.

He has his own world, his own friends, his own thoughts.

Sometimes I have to ask twice to get a full sentence. 😄

And yet… in that
 one small moment, with his arm around my shoulder, I could still feel my little boy hiding inside this growing young man.

Nobody prepares you for this stage of motherhood.

You spend years wishing they would grow up.

Then one day they do.
And suddenly you realise you would give anything to hold on to these tiny flashes of childhood that still visit you for a few seconds at a time.

So today I’m not posting a perfect photo.
I’m posting a reminder to myself:

Don’t miss the 5-second moments while waiting for the big milestones. 💛
Because sometimes motherhood lives in a quick side hug, a half smile, and an arm around your shoulder that disappears before you’re ready to let it go.

💬 Moms of teenagers — what is the one small thing your child still does that melts your heart every single time?
posts.hook: “The arm around my shoulder lasted 5 seconds… and I wanted to freeze time.”

posts.text:
I snapped at my son over a wet towel on the bed.

It wasn't about the towel.

As the mother of a teenager, I know the eye-roll, the closed door, the "Mumma, chill."

And honestly?
Some days my patience runs out faster than his.

For a long time I thought that made me a worse mother.

Then I started looking at it as a hormone health coach.

In your late 30s and 40s, progesterone often starts dropping first, sometimes years before your periods change.
Progesterone is your calming hormone.
When it dips, many women notice:
a shorter fuse,
lighter sleep,
anxiety that comes out of nowhere,
crying at an ad and then feeling silly about it.

Now add a teenager who is learning to be his own person.
Two bodies going through big hormonal shifts under one roof. 😄

That is not bad parenting.
That is biology meeting real life.

What helps me:
- protecting my sleep like it's a client appointment
- protein at breakfast, so I'm not running on chai and fumes
- strength training 4 days a week, my best stress outlet
- saying "I need 5 minutes" before I say something I regret

He still rolls his eyes.
But every now and then, he still puts his arm around me without being asked.
I'll take it. 

Moms of teenagers, what tests your patience the most right now?
posts.hook: I snapped at my son over a wet towel on the bed.

𝐇𝐞 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲𝐨𝐧𝐞. 𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐇𝐢𝐦?

He pays the EMIs. 
He drives his parents to every appointment. 
He's the first to show up when anyone needs anything.

When did anyone last ask how he's doing?

I coach women. But I see the men in the background of their stories.

The husband awake at 2 AM doing the maths on school fees, the home loan and his fathers medical bills. Who says Im fine the next morning and goes back to work.

Nobody taught him a different sentence.

Boys learn early: don't cry, handle it, be the strong one. By 40, he's an expert at carrying and a beginner at asking. 

His body keeps the account. 

Chronic stress keeps cortisol up and sleep short. In one well-known study, healthy young men who slept five hours a night for a week had 10-15% lower daytime testosterone. Add rising blood pressure, belly fat and blood sugar. South Asian men also tend to develop heart disease years earlier than men elsewhere. 

And he won't tell you. Many men see a doctor only after something is already broken.   

𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐚𝐬 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝. 

Here's the part I find most striking.

The woman who is everyones emergency contact is very often married to the man who is everyones silent provider. Two exhausted people in one house, each quietly assuming the other has it easier.

If you love a man like this, three small things: 

1. Ask How are you actually doing? Then ask it a second time. The first answer is always fine.
2. Book the annual check-up he keeps postponing: blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, vitamin D, B12, thyroid.
3. Protect his sleep like a medical treatment. It is one. 

𝘐𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶'𝘳𝘦 𝘢 𝘸𝘰𝘮𝘢𝘯 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴, 𝘴𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘵 𝘵𝘰 him.If 𝘺𝘰𝘶'𝘳𝘦 𝘩𝘪𝘮, 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘮𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘴𝘭𝘪𝘱.

𝐍𝐚𝐯𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐫𝐢 𝐭𝐨 𝐃𝐢𝐰𝐚𝐥𝐢: 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐨 𝐄𝐚𝐭, 𝐒𝐥𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐇𝐲𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐧 𝐍𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫

𝘐𝘍𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴𝘯'𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮.
𝘈𝘭𝘭-𝘰𝘳-𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘴.
"𝘐'𝘭𝘭 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯 𝘢𝘧𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘋𝘪𝘸𝘢𝘭𝘪" 𝘪𝘴 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘯 𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘴𝘪𝘹 𝘸𝘦𝘦𝘬𝘴.

Between now and the end of the festive season, you'll have fasts, feasts, late nights and sweets in every kitchen. You don't need a strict plan. You need three anchors.

𝟏. 𝐄𝐀𝐓𝐈𝐍𝐆

Don't save up for the feast. Skipping breakfast and lunch to "make room" sends blood sugar on a rollercoaster, and by evening your body is begging for sugar.

Eat protein and vegetables first, sweets after, never on an empty stomach. Protein and fibre before carbohydrate lowers the glucose spike.

Fasting days: sabudana, potato and kuttu are mostly starch. Pair them with paneer, curd, makhana or nuts so you don't crash by 4 PM. Break the fast with protein, not only sweets.

Walk 10–15 minutes after the big meal. It is the simplest tool we have for lowering the post-meal glucose rise.

𝟐. 𝐒𝐋𝐄𝐄𝐏

One short night raises hunger and cravings the next day. Late nights are coming, so protect one thing: your wake-up time, within an hour of normal.

Make up the sleep the next night; don't cover it with caffeine all day.

Alcohol and heavy meals close to bedtime fragment sleep. Eat dinner earlier on the nights you can.

𝟑. 𝐇𝐘𝐃𝐑𝐀𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍

Festive food is salty, sweet and fried, and you'll be sweating in the kitchen. Start the day with water before chai, keep a bottle where you can see it, and add electrolytes (a pinch of salt and lemon, or ORS) on fasting days and heavy-sweat days.

The day after: don't punish. No fasting, no extra workout. The next meal is a normal meal. One day of mithai doesn't undo months. The reset mindset does.

On thyroid medication? Take it on an empty stomach, and keep calcium, iron and heavy dairy sweets about 4 hours away from it.

𝘐𝘚𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘋𝘪𝘸𝘢𝘭𝘪 𝘸𝘦𝘦𝘬. 𝘈𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘦𝘭𝘭 𝘮𝘦: 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘤𝘩 𝘴𝘸𝘦𝘦𝘵 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘨𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘶𝘱?

For two years, she did everything “right.”
Iron tablets. A haematologist. Regular blood tests.

📍 Ferritin — March 2024: 5.18
📍 Ferritin — July 2026: 6.30

Two years of effort, and it moved by about one point.
When she came to me, her haemoglobin was 9.8.
She was tired, her hair was falling, and she had quietly accepted that her body was “just like this.”
Nobody had asked her one question:

Is the iron actually getting in?

Here's something important to understand:
Swallowing iron doesn't mean you absorb it.
Your gut has to take it in, and your daily routine can quietly interfere with that process.
So we didn't start by adding more iron.

We looked at what was getting in the way.

Here's what we addressed. 👇
🔎 1. GUT FIRST
We addressed her gut health and completed a deworming course before expecting absorption to improve.
⏰ 2. TIMING MATTERS
She was taking iron one hour after her thyroid tablet.
The two interfere with each other, and the usual advice is to keep them at least 4 hours apart.
She discovered this herself, and we moved her iron to dinner.
🔄 3. EVERY OTHER DAY
Studies show that alternate-day iron dosing can improve absorption in some circumstances.

Why?

A daily dose increases a hormone called hepcidin, which can temporarily reduce iron absorption from the next dose.

🥗 4. THE RIGHT FOOD RULES
We separated iron from tea, coffee and calcium, but not from all food.
She had been skipping meals around her iron supplementation and crashing as a result.
And then came the follow-up report.

✨ Nine weeks later, her ferritin was 34.62.
Look at the difference:
📊 Two years: +1
📊 Nine weeks: +28

When I shared the report, she barely reacted.
After two years of disappointment, I understood why.
One good number doesn't undo years of being let down.
She's not "done" yet.
We're aiming for 70+.
The same retest also showed that her thyroid needed attention, so she went back to her endocrinologist, who adjusted her dose.
And that's how it should work.
Coach and doctor. Each doing their part.
But the lesson stands.
If you've been on iron for months and your numbers won't move, the answer is rarely just "take more."
Ask what’s stopping it from getting in.
👇 If this sounds like your reports, comment "IRON" and I'll tell you what to check first.
#WomensHealth #IronDeficiency #Ferritin #ThyroidHealth #HormonalHealth
